extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and lawyers handling equitable relief for patent infringement (and advanced law students)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and discretionary standards courts apply when deciding whether to grant, dissolve, or suspend injunctions to restrain patent infringement (interlocutory and at final hearing). Covers factors like possession/use, prior recoveries, conflicting evidence, effect on defendant, and procedural posture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie right to an interlocutory injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a prima facie right to an injunction, without a trial at law, upon certain things being shown, namely, a patent, long possession, and infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patentee must furnish some further evidence of a probable right beyond the mere issue of the patent; long undisturbed use and exercise of the patent strengthens the probability and often justifies issuing an injunction in aid of it (cases cited: Orr v. Littlefield, Neilson v. Thompson, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of long enjoyment and prior recoveries on presumption of validity
rubrics_metrics.description: When the presumption in favor of the validity of the patent has been strengthened by evidence of enjoyment and possession undisturbed for several years, and recoveries against others for violating it, affidavits tending to cast doubts on originality will not suffice to deprive the plaintiff of an injunction before trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long, uninterrupted possession, extensive and profitable sales, and prior recoveries or licenses (if not collusive) are strong public assurances that the patent is good; such circumstances can trump respondent affidavits in a preliminary inquiry. The court treats such possession and judgments together in support of an injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to weigh when respondent adduces opposing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When opposing evidence is adduced by the respondent, courts weigh: how far, and how long, there has been exclusive possession or assertion of the right; how far the respondent has raised doubts as to novelty, patentable subject, or infringement; and how far long possession counteracts evidence impeaching validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elements guide the court's discretion in deciding whether the plaintiff's prima facie right has been displaced so as to suspend an injunction until the plaintiff establishes the right by action. The inquiry is cautious where evidence is taken without cross-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicting evidence on possession and novelty — injunction refused until trial
rubrics_metrics.description: If the respondent succeeds in raising doubts both as to the exclusive possession and as to the novelty of what is claimed, and the evidence on these points is conflicting, the injunction will be refused until a trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A substantial, conflicting factual record on possession and novelty displaces the interlocutory remedy and requires he trial at law to resolve those disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubt as to infringement — jury trial required; injunction may be dissolved
rubrics_metrics.description: If the question of infringement is doubtful, it must be tried by a jury; the court may dissolve an injunction and order an action to try the infringement (with conditions like accounts to be kept and admission of title).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule applies both to dissolution of existing injunctions and as a constraint on granting interlocutory injunctions when infringement is a matter of factual uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of harms / effect on defendant's business (irreparable harm to defendant)
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of the injunction on the defendant's business is an element to be considered; where irreparable mischief would ensue to the defendant, an injunction ought not to be granted — provided the plaintiff would not be injured by the delay or can be protected by an account kept in the interim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The grant of an injunction is discretionary and aims to prevent mischief; courts consider whether the plaintiff can be made whole by later relief (e.g., account of profits) before enjoining defendant activities that would cause irreparable business harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff's conduct: acquiescence, expense incurred, estoppel, and laches
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will not be granted where the plaintiff has permitted the defendant to go on and incur expense under the expectation of receiving a certain sum, if the relations between them allow the defendant to dispute the plaintiff's right; but if the defendant is estopped at law from denying validity, an injunction will be granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If real questions remain and defendant has incurred substantial reliance costs, the court may require payment into court (e.g., year's rent due) or refuse injunction; equitable doctrines (estoppel/laches) affect relief. Courts balance these equitable considerations when exercising discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual infringement plus necessary possession -> injunction despite defendant promises
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plaintiff shows the necessary possession, and an infringement has actually been committed by the defendant, the injunction will be granted notwithstanding the defendant admits the infringement and promises not to repeat it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere promise by the defendant not to repeat wrongful acts is insufficient to protect plaintiff's rights once infringement and possession are established; the court will still enjoin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different, stricter approach at final hearing (delay and failure to seek interlocutory relief)
rubrics_metrics.description: At the final hearing the court examines objections to validity differently; if the plaintiff had opportunity to seek interlocutory relief and neglected it (or has allowed the suit to remain pending for a long time), the court may refuse to grant relief and may dismiss the bill with costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plaintiff who brings a cause to hearing is expected to have it in a state enabling adjudication; failure to seek earlier legal determination of title may be fatal at hearing. Courts disfavor plaintiffs who delay and thereby cause prejudice or unnecessary uncertainty to defendants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to pursue trial at law when possession/exercise is insufficient or patent has gross defects
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff will be sent to try his title at law, without a previous injunction, if he does not show long possession and exercise of his exclusive right; where the injunction is resisted by evidence which casts doubt on originality or usefulness of the patent; or where the patent contains gross and obvious defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Defects' mean doubts as to originality or usefulness or errors in specification; where such doubts exist, equitable aid is withheld pending legal determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: No fixed temporal standard for 'long possession' — practical commercial test
rubrics_metrics.description: No specific lapse of time is adopted as a universal standard; the general principle is that the time elapsed must have been sufficient to permit articles or machines to be constructed by the patentee in conformity with his claim, and to be sold publicly and repeatedly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court looks to practical evidence: construction, public sales, repeated use — not to an arbitrary number of years. Short periods have sufficed where actual use and sales occurred; in some cases a few years (even 3–6) have been enough if accompanied by public use and sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public sales and the nature of possession relied on
rubrics_metrics.description: If public sale is the kind of possession relied on, it must in fact have been sold publicly; former recoveries or licenses relied on as proof of possession must not appear collusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recoveries and submissions obtained by agreement without initial real contest may fail to prove possession. Evidence of licences and recoveries must be scrutinized for genuineness; affidavits offered in preliminary inquiries are unsafe where cross-examination lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior recoveries/licenses must be under the same patent or legally connected patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Where former use or former recoveries are relied upon as proof of possession of the exclusive right, they must have been under the same patent, or under a patent connected in law with that under which the application is made; otherwise they will not show they related to the same right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under systems of amending specifications or surrendering and reissuing patents, a new patent may be legally connected to the old so prior possession under the old patent will support an injunction under the amended patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicting patents between parties — injunction withheld until rights tried at law
rubrics_metrics.description: Where both parties claim under patents (conflicting patents apparently for the same thing), the court cannot grant an injunction until the rights have been tried at law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Undisturbed possession grounds for injunction cannot exist when two conflicting patents both claim the same subject; equitable relief is deferred to avoid deciding substantive title when both assert competing patent rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's discretion to require further investigation (action at law or issue out of chancery)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plaintiff has made out a prima facie case by proof of possession and enjoyment, the court must consider whether the nature of the case entitles the defendant to further investigation into validity or infringement; defendant has a right to further investigation where there are questions of fact or law that equity does not ordinarily settle, and the investigation will generally be ordered to take place in an action at law (though the court may direct an issue out of chancery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when prima facie grounds for an interlocutory injunction exist, the court may exercise discretion to send legal questions to a jury or law court if the matters fall outside equity's usual remit; courts weigh the need for a full trial against the risk of irreparable harm to the patentee.
